title: Addiction and recovery
hook: one day at a time, with help and grace
tomorrow: Peter swore he'd never fail. so what happened after he did?

segments.voice: Yesterday, when a marriage ends: still in the family, with a place at the table. Today, a different kind of ending, and a beginning that comes one morning at a time.
screen: `STILL IN THE FAMILY.` → `ONE MORNING AT A TIME.`

segments.voice: Is "one day at a time" in the Bible, or just a slogan? The words are a saying from recovery groups. The idea is far older. Anyone who has tried to quit something knows the bargain: just get through this week, this month, the rest of your life. In Exodus there is a man who tries to do the rest of his life in advance. Last night he scraped extra bread into a pot and hid it in his tent, because what if tomorrow there is nothing? Now it is dawn in the desert, and he lifts the lid on his backup plan. It is full of worms, and it stinks.
screen: `IN THE BIBLE, OR A SLOGAN?` → `EXTRA BREAD, HIDDEN IN A TENT.` → `BY MORNING, IT STINKS.`

segments.voice: So why would God send bread that won't keep? The bread is manna, and the rule comes with it: gather what you need for the day. Kept overnight, it spoils. The people have to trust there will be more tomorrow, and there is. Jesus puts that same rhythm into the prayer he teaches. In the Douay-Rheims Bible: "Give us this day our supersubstantial bread." This day, not this year. A few lines later: "Sufficient for the day is the evil thereof." So the saying sounds like it came straight out of that desert. Something to tell a friend tonight: some recovery groups meet in parish halls, folding chairs under a crucifix. And recovery isn't treated as willpower alone. Help counts: a sponsor, a doctor, a meeting, a friend who picks up at two in the morning. Grace counts too. Paul begged God to take away something painful he never names, and the answer he heard was: "My grace is sufficient for thee." Not a cure on the spot. Enough for today. Recovery doesn't ask anyone to be well forever by Friday. It asks for today, with help, then tomorrow, with help again. And when someone slips, the desert story has a word for that too: the bread still came the next morning.
screen: `MANNA: ENOUGH FOR THE DAY.` · `GIVE US THIS DAY.` · `HELP COUNTS, AND GRACE COUNTS.` · `THE BREAD CAME AGAIN.` · then, large: `ONE DAY AT A TIME.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind someone in recovery, or someone you hope will get there; it can be you. Say their name quietly, then three words: just for today. If you pray, you can add the line from the Our Father for them, give us this day our daily bread, and let the rest of the sit be for their today.
Addiction and recovery. Something that takes hold of a life, and the long road back, walked a day at a time, with help and grace.
Your line: one day at a time. The manna came again the next morning. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Catholics pray the Our Father, with its "give us this day," at every Mass and in daily prayer; some parishes open their halls to recovery groups, and priests and parish ministers walk with people in recovery through prayer and the sacraments.

fork.setup: your uncle is newly sober and says he has to stay sober for the rest of his life, starting now. it's crushing him. what does the manna story offer?
options: only today's portion: get through today, with help.
plan every week ahead so nothing catches him off guard.

fork.reveal: manna was gathered for one day, and Jesus taught people to ask for bread this day. one day at a time, with help and grace.

original.note: Greek, from Matthew 6:11: the word behind "daily" or "supersubstantial" bread; its exact sense is debated.

trapdoor: what you thought: one day at a time is just a recovery slogan.
what it means: the old rhythm of manna and the Our Father: enough for today, with help, then again tomorrow.
what a scholar hears: Exodus 16's manna that won't keep; the debated Greek epiousios in Matthew 6:11 (Douay: supersubstantial); 2 Corinthians 12:9's grace that is sufficient.
guess: being hooked on something, and the road back
a weak will that just needs more effort
a bad habit you fix with one decision

chat.says: Val's brother Nico is home from rehab. he messed up last time. ok but does recovery actually work?
options: Not all at once. It works a day at a time, with help, and a slip isn't the end.
Only if he's strong enough this time. Real recovery is willpower, not other people.
If he prays hard enough it should just go away, so tell Val to pray more.
chat.meaning: Like manna, recovery is taken a day at a time, with help and grace. Nobody has to be well forever by Friday.

manna.meaning: the bread from heaven Israel gathered each morning in the desert

Exodus.meaning: the book of the Bible telling Israel's escape from Egypt

Douay-Rheims.meaning: an old English Catholic translation of the Bible

Paul.meaning: an early apostle who wrote letters to the first churches

Our Father.meaning: the Lord's Prayer, the prayer Jesus taught

notes: Matthew 6:11, 6:34 and 2 Corinthians 12:9 quoted from Douay-Rheims (Challoner); confirm exact wording.

Exodus 16 paraphrased: gather each day's portion; manna left until morning bred worms and stank (16:19–20). The man hiding bread in his tent is a retelling of 'some of them left of it until the morning'; confirm the retelling is fair.
'One day at a time' is presented as a saying of recovery groups, not a Bible quotation; 'some of those groups meet in parish halls' is hedged. Confirm.
Epiousios (Matthew 6:11): its meaning is debated; Douay renders 'supersubstantial'. Confirm the Greek and the note.
For parents: the lesson names addiction and rehab gently, with no detail; suitable for a family listen.
